newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese government's 1997 budget draws MPs' fire.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese government's 1997 budget draws MPs' fire.

text.p: The Lebanese parliament opened on Wednesday its 1997 state budget debate with deputies criticising the government's planned tight deficit as unrealistic.

Most MPs who spoke on the first day of the four-day debate said they doubted the government would meet its goal of slashing the deficit of revenue against expenditure in the current year's budget to about 36 percent.
Some MPs said there was a wastage of public funds and urged the government to rationalise its spending while others warned against the problem of mushrooming public debt.

"The government is accustomed to giving us figures that are overly optimistic...From past experience, we will not be surprised if this (1997 deficit) will reach 50 percent," MP Selim el-Hoss, a former prime minister, said.

The government sees the tight 1997 budget as an attempt to slash Lebanon's massive budget deficits, which are partly caused by heavy spending on Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's multi-billion dollar postwar reconstruction programme.

But it has failed to keep planned deficits in recent previous years under control. The 1996 deficit, planned at 2,428 billion Lebanese pounds or 38 percent of expenditure, in fact ended up at 3,692 billion pounds or 51 percent.

The original 1997 budget draft approved by the government last September proposed expenditures of about 6,400 billion pounds against income of 4,100 billion -- or a 35.9 percent shortfall. But the government approved on Saturday a net increase in proposed spending of 33 billion.

Acting finance minister Fouad Siniora said last September that the government's aim was to tighten spending in 1997, adding the budget will relax financial markets and give different economic sectors easier access to sources of finance.

The MPs dismissed officials' claims that the wide margin between the planned and actual 1996 deficit was largely due to the 17-day Israeli blitz last April which caused massive damage and thus boosted emergency spending.
"There is a wastage in public spending that can not be underestimated and part of it is manifested in administrative corruption," Hoss said.
Parliament's finance and budget committee also criticised the budget, especially warning against the problem of ballooning debt saying it was nearing gross domestic product.
"The net public debt of $10.6 billion is nearing the estimated gross domestic product which induces high debt servicing on the treasury," MP Khalil al-Hrawi, who heads the committee, said.
More than 42 percent of 1997 spending will go to debt servicing and interest -- some 100 billion pounds up on last year -- and about 35 percent will go to salaries and wages.
